Elysium: Simulation-Free Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridges
summary: Reconstructing cellular dynamics from snapshots is challenging because the destructive nature of single-cell measurements makes tracking the same cells over time impossible. Cellular dynamics are inherently stochastic and involve changes in population size through proliferation and apoptosis. Growth-based methods represent population change as a rate on the density, which does not assign exits and entries to individual cells. Unbalanced Schrödinger bridges model individual events, but neural solvers for killed diffusion bridges simulate trajectories during training. We introduce Elysium, a simulation-free solver that jointly learns state transition and mass change. Using a killed Brownian reference and its time reversal, Elysium constructs direct regression objectives from an optimal endpoint coupling and conditional bridge distributions, without simulating trajectories during training. We show that the minimizers of the expected training objectives recover the optimal unbalanced Schrödinger bridge. Empirically, Elysium reconstructs state transitions, population size, and event distributions on simulated benchmarks with known killed-diffusion ground truth, outperforming existing deterministic and bridge-based solvers. On single-cell time courses, it interpolates cell state distributions at unobserved time points, tracks population expansion and contraction, and captures biphasic drug-response dynamics.

Plasma biomarkers of Alzheimer's disease reveal conserved features of age-related neurodegeneration in chimpanzees and humans
summary: Aging is a major risk factor for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD). Yet, the physiological relationships linking age-related changes in peripheral biomarkers and measures of brain structure have only recently begun to be explored. Nonhuman primates, whose brains naturally express some of the pathologic hallmarks of AD/ADRD, including amyloid-beta (A{beta}) plaques, vascular amyloid, and neurofibrillary tangles, represent a critical translational bridge between rodent models and humans. Here, we utilized ultrasensitive multiplex assays and structural MRI to examine the relationship of plasma AD/ADRD biomarkers with age, sex, and whole brain cortical thickness (CT) and gray matter volume (GMV) in a cohort of chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), humans' closest extant living relatives. Plasma levels (pg/ml) of total tau, phosphorylated tau 217 (pTau217), A{beta}40, A{beta}42, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and neurofilament light chain (NfL) were measured in a cross-sectional sample of 154 chimpanzees ranging from 12-57 years of age. As in humans, aging was associated with increased plasma total tau, pTau217, A{beta}40, A{beta}42, GFAP, and NfL levels, as well as reduced whole brain CT and GMV in chimpanzees. The ratio of plasma A{beta}42/A{beta}40 increased with age in male chimpanzees, whereas aging was not significantly associated with the ratio of pTau217/A{beta}42. Mediation analyses revealed that age-related increases in plasma A{beta}42 mediated whole brain GMV atrophy in chimpanzees. Together, these findings demonstrate that plasma AD/ADRD biomarkers and measures of brain structure undergo age-related changes in chimpanzees, which is highly relevant to the study of human aging and AD/ADRD.

title: Bidirectional acetate exchange couples ethanol turnover to acetyl-CoA metabolism in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
summary: Overflow metabolism describes the excretion of partially oxidized metabolites into the extracellular environment during rapid sugar utilization. Although these metabolites can later be reused, it remains unclear whether reassimilation also occurs during ongoing sugar consumption, and if so, how. Here, 13C-isotope tracing and metabolic flux analysis of acetate exchange in Saccharomyces cerevisiae during hexose utilization reveal that net acetate overflow is only the small difference between order-of-magnitude larger simultaneous excretion and assimilation fluxes. Unlike ethanol production, acetate exchange is not determined by hexose uptake but depends on metabolic processes downstream of glycolysis. Ethanol oxidation contributes to acetate excretion even during net ethanol production, directly linking the two main overflow pathways. We exploited this understanding to redirect extracellular acetate into the acetyl-CoA-derived product mevalonate. These results establish acetate overflow as a dynamic exchange linking ethanol turnover to acetyl-CoA metabolism, in which acetate is simultaneously an overflow product and a carbon source that can be redirected toward bioproduction.

title: N- and T-genes framework for pathway deregulation: Taxonomy, progression, and protection in cancer
summary: Background. Pathway analysis is widely used to interpret gene expression, but conventional enrichment depends on arbitrary thresholds and does not quantify deregulation magnitude. Recent reformulations based on average log-fold changes remove the threshold but still average over all annotated genes, diluting the signal from the genes that actually drive the normal-to-tumor transition. The N/T framework, which identifies genes with exclusive expression intervals in normal (N) or tumor (T) samples, offers a selective alternative, but it had not been extended to pathway- level quantification, taxonomy, or cross-cancer comparison. Methods. We define effective activation frequencies for Reactome pathways based on N- and T-genes: for each sample and pathway, the effective N (T) frequency is the fraction of annotated N (T) genes active in a normal (tumor) sample. The analysis proceeds in three explicit steps: (i) cohort averages identify the pathways important in each tissue; (ii) averages over hierarchical-clustering groups, ordered by the number of active genes, reveal sequences of pathway activation and deactivation along progression; (iii) a minimum spanning tree (MST) built on pathway-frequency vectors -- independent of the number of active genes -- defines the molecular taxonomy, and branch averages identify subtype-specific programs. We apply the framework to the full set of Reactome pathways in prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC), and glioblastoma (GBM), analyzing both tumor and normal compartments. Results. In PRAD tumors (n=499), hierarchical clustering identifies four ordered progression groups and the MST resolves six main molecular subtypes comprising 406 tumors (81.4%): B1 (42.1%; MET/NFE2L2/energy metabolism), B2 (13.8%; RAS/apoptosis/telomere), and four smaller subtypes defined by PTEN (B3), DNA repair and lipid metabolism (B4), inflammation and LXR-mediated lipid metabolism (B5), and neuronal development and base excision repair (B6). An eight-gene perfect T panel reproduces the MST subtypes at gene level. Analysis of normal prostatic tissue (n=52) reveals a hierarchy of protection: immune response, apoptosis, and senescence are lost or partially lost early, DNA repair at an intermediate stage, and cell cycle regulation and receptor tyrosine kinase signaling last; an eleven-gene N panel reproduces this hierarchy at gene level. The cross-cancer comparison shows that this architecture is a general property: DNA repair, cell cycle, and RTK protection are maintained in normal tissue across PRAD, LUAD, LIHC, and GBM, while the specific pathways lost in normals and gained in tumors are tissue-specific (MET/NFE2L2 in PRAD; NTRK/LXR/phagosome in LIHC; surfactant/FGFR/glycosylation in LUAD; TP53loss/lipid metabolism/glycosylation in GBM). Taxonomic heterogeneity decreases from PRAD (six subtypes) to LIHC (two) to LUAD and GBM (one dominant program), paralleling an increase in the number of activated T-genes. Conclusions. The framework eliminates dilution by non-nformative genes, quantifies pathway deregulation sample by sample, and unifies tumor taxonomy with a molecular indicator of progression. Its most distinctive contribution is the joint analysis of normal and tumor compartments across cancer types, which links loss of protection in normal tissue to gain of progression programs in tumors and reveals both shared and tissue-specific cancer mechanisms. The method is general and applicable across cancer types, although quantitative results depend on the underlying cohort.

title: Scalable biophysical constraints link steady-state and kinetic metabolic modeling
summary: Rational metabolic engineering relies on models that connect molecular mechanisms to cellular behavior. Constraint-based metabolic models integrate stoichiometric, thermodynamic, and omics-derived information, but they do not generally constrain whether flux magnitudes are compatible with the corresponding metabolite pool sizes. Metabolite turnover rates, the ratios of total production or consumption flux to pool size, capture this relationship and quantify how rapidly pools are renewed. Without turnover constraints, such models can admit flux-concentration combinations with implausible pool-renewal timescales despite satisfying mass balance and thermodynamics. We present METEOR-K, a scalable framework that couples steady-state fluxes and metabolite concentrations through turnover-rate constraints and turnover-aware sampling. These constraints encode physiological timescales or experimental turnover estimates, either network-wide or for selected metabolites. We applied METEOR-K to a reduced glycolysis pathway, two Escherichia coli networks, one anaerobic and one aerobic, and near-genome-scale ovarian cancer metabolism. Across these systems, METEOR-K narrowed the admissible steady-state space, reduced flux-concentration uncertainty, and shifted kinetic ensembles toward faster local dynamics and physiologically compatible responses. Nonlinear simulations yielded E. coli growth behavior consistent with experimental observations and supported perturbation recovery in the ovarian cancer model. In the aerobic E. coli core model, literature-derived turnover intervals for 18 metabolites narrowed flux and concentration ranges across the network, increased the fraction of locally stable models from 26.8% to 73.5%, and shortened median relaxation times by over four orders of magnitude relative to the unconstrained reference. METEOR-K provides turnover-consistent steady states for constraint-based analyses and physiologically grounded reference states for kinetic modeling and model-guided metabolic engineering.

title: From CSP7 to CSP5: Development of a soluble, truncated congener for the treatment of obstructive and restrictive lung diseases.
summary: Chronic obstructive and restrictive lung diseases (CLDs), represent a substantial worldwide health burden, with curative therapies remaining largely unavailable. Studies from our group and others have identified caveolin-1 (Cav1)-mediated signaling as a critical regulator of cellular processes implicated in the pathogenesis and progression of CLDs, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), silicosis and other progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PF) conditions. We have previously demonstrated that Cav1 scaffolding domain peptides (CSP and CSP7), attenuate lung injury and PF across multiple preclinical mouse models and exhibit protective and anti-fibrotic effects in COPD and IPF tissues ex vivo. The mechanism involves concurrent suppression of p53 and its downstream signaling in lung (airway and alveolar) epithelial cells by competitively counteracting excess Cav1, while restoring baseline p53 levels in (myo)fibroblasts persisting in fibrotic lungs, and alternatively polarized alveolar macrophages (AMs) by complementing Cav1 function. The safety and tolerability of inhaled micronized CSP7 dry powder (aka LTI-03), have been evaluated in mice, rats, dogs, followed by a Phase 1a clinical trial assessing safety and pharmacokinetics in healthy volunteers (NCT04233814) and a Phase 1b trial in patients with IPF (NCT05954988). LTI-03 has subsequently advanced to a multicenter Phase 2 clinical trial in patients with IPF (NCT06968845). However, the FDA highlighted findings of minimal bronchiolar mucus cell metaplasia and hyperplasia in the 26-week rat inhalation study, raisings concerns regarding the suitability of poorly soluble CSP7 for long-term administration in patients with CLDs, particularly for COPD, a disease already characterized by goblet cell metaplasia and hyperplasia, mucus hypersecretion, impaired mucociliary clearance, and small airway obstruction. To address these limitations, we identified CSP5, a five amino acid truncated derivative of CSP7. Notably, the amorphous CSP5 attenuated p53 activation and apoptosis in preclinical models of tobacco smoke (TS)-, bleomycin, and silica-induced lung injury, demonstrating its potential to protect against epithelial injury across diverse lung disease models. Additionally, CSP5 enhanced surfactant protein C expression, consistent with alveolar epithelial cell homeostasis and regeneration, while suppressing Mucin 5Ac expression and attenuating distal lung injury in mice chronically exposed to TS. Furthermore, CSP5 promoted resolution of established PF in mouse models of bleomycin- or silica-induced fibrosis. CSP7, encompassing the CSP5 sequence, attenuates autophagic dysregulation, endoplasmic reticulum stress, reactive oxygen species, mitochondrial membrane potential abnormalities, and mitochondrial superoxide production, and profibrotic polarization of AMs in mice with PF. Collectively, these findings position CSP5 as a formidable next-generation peptide with preserved bioactive motif of CSP7 while offering improved physicochemical and potential advantages in formulation flexibility. The dominant features of CSP5 support its further development for chronic inhaled or systemic administration in the treatment of obstructive or fibrotic lung diseases.
